answers.justification: C5 matched claim rates for Pellacott 2026 valves are the same for legacy and new installers (41 vs 42), and Durrant-Hale sits at 5–7 in every installer group; brazed joints were intact on all 41 teardowns, never-installed warehouse valves leak at 11% (C5), and C1 shows new firms were trained with few findings, so E1/E5/C4/C6 are confounded by build year.

C10 found LT-04 out of service since 9 Jan 2026 with no test cycle after 18 Dec 2025, no VA-220 program on any other rig and no backup rig, and the 2026 per-piece tables repeat four sequences from Nov 2025, yet E6 claims LT-04 tested a July 2026 lot; C5 shows the 2026 valves are defective.

The tests recorded on the certificates could not have been run, because the only VA-220 rig had been out of service since January and the tables are copied sequences (C10), so 'tested but the method missed the defect' does not fit; C5 notes the pressure-decay method was not replicated, but the tests were never actually done.

C5 shows Pellacott 2026 valves fail at about the same rate on firmware 4.1 (40) and 4.2 (42), Durrant-Hale stays at 5–7 on both, E2 shows the rise had started with Jan–Feb builds before the 10 Mar rollout, and C2 validation found no valve faults.

C8/E3 show that conformance scores rose across the programme (71 to 96) and that no supplier's rig logs are collected, so the claim cannot be ruled out, but no evidence shows fabrication by any supplier other than Pellacott.

Warehouse retest of never-installed valves (C5: Pellacott 2026 11% vs 2025 1% vs Durrant-Hale 0%), teardown showing seal-seat failure matching the dominant claim code (E2), installer, firmware and weather rivals ruled out (C5, C12), a claims-coding artefact excluded (C7), and timing matching the Jan 2026 changes (E4, E2).
C5 shows identical failure rates by installer group for both valve sources, and brazed joints were intact (C5, C6 'no burn marks').
C5 shows no firmware difference within valve source (40 vs 42; Durrant-Hale 5–7 in every group), and the rise starts in builds from before March (E2).

Seal deformation co-occurs with 2026 Corlin-sealed valves (C5, C11 untested compression set and harder-to-softer compound change), but C5 states the Corlin seal and the Line 3 move cannot be separated and the compound was not analysed.

By the E3 formula, conformance rising 58 to 100 at 0.40 weight contributes about 17 of the 19-point gain, while audit (74 to 79) and delivery barely moved, so the score rise follows mechanically from the record change (C13, C8).

With falsified certificates (C10) and an 11% seat-leak rate in uninstalled 2026 stock (C5), containment, suspending dock-to-stock and Brenmoor-run helium testing (which detected the defect in C5) protect the field.
C5 shows installers are not the cause, so suspending installers and charging claims back to them punishes the wrong party (C1 shows they were trained and audited).

Fresh certificates from Pellacott are worthless, because its certificates reflect no actual tests (C10), and about 11% of 2026 lots leak (C5), so releasing the lots would put defective valves into the field.
The seal-source cause is confounded with the Line 3 move and the compound was not analysed (C5, C11), so mandating Ferrand is not yet justified, though it may prove right.

Requiring rig logs or witnessed tests fixes the loophole Pellacott exploited (C8, C13, E3), but leaving 14 other suppliers' dock-to-stock grants unverified until 18 Dec (C8), when the programme verifies no raw test data, keeps a known weakness open, so this is not a best action.

Independent rig observation (C10) plus warehouse retest and matched claim breakdown (C5) are enough to commit to A1 containment and suspension now, even though root cause (seal vs Line 3) is still open.

ambiguousItems: I15: 'acceptable' vs 'harmful' — the clause leaving other suppliers' dock-to-stock grants unverified until the next cycle could be read as keeping a protective control disabled despite a demonstrated way to game the programme.
I9: 'association-only' vs 'unknown' — the seal and Line 3 are fully confounded, so the link to the seal specifically could be judged not even shown.
I3: 'contradicted' vs 'unknown' — the pressure-decay method was never replicated (C5), but C10 shows no tests were run, so the H3 premise is false.
caseProblems: E6 says LT-04 calibration is due 30 Nov 2026 on a July 2026 certificate while C10 shows LT-04 failed in Jan 2026; this contradiction is intended, but it already hints at H2 before C10 is read.

C10's catalogue title ('Calibration contractor site-visit report, Pellacott leak-test rigs') is neutral, but its contents alone almost settle H2 and H3; C5 also settles H1, H4, R2 and R3 in one item, which makes the case depend heavily on two decisive items.
C8 lists 15 suppliers with dock-to-stock and E3 covers 22 suppliers, but H5 has no discriminating evidence at all, so its answer can only be 'unknown' by design.

rulings.explanation: 'Harmful' requires an action likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control. A5 disables nothing. Other suppliers' dock-to-stock grants are already in place, so the deferral clause keeps the status quo for a few weeks (the cycle closes 18 Dec 2026, per C8). The new scoring rule adds a verification control that does not exist today. Nothing in the evidence shows that any other supplier's records are false: H5 stays unknown, and C8 notes the programme collects no raw data. So the evidence does not show that leaving those grants in place briefly is likely to worsen outcomes. 'Preferred' also fails. The deferral clause openly leaves a demonstrated gaming route unchecked when immediate verification was possible, and A5 does nothing about the defective stock that A1 contains. That makes it a reasonable systemic fix that is not among the best next actions, so 'acceptable' is the only defensible answer. The flagged reading treats keeping an already-disabled control in place as disabling it, which the definition of 'harmful' does not cover.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, add to the I15 rationale that A5 removes no control that exists today and that H5 is unknown, so the deferral cannot be called likely to worsen outcomes.

rulings.explanation: 'Unknown' means the evidence cannot even show association. Here association is clearly shown. The Corlin seal switch took effect with the first 2026 run (E4). 2026-built never-installed Pellacott valves leak at the seat at 11%, against 1 in 100 for 2025-built and 0 for Durrant-Hale (C5). Teardowns put the defect in the deformed, unseated slide seal (C5). Being fully confounded with Line 3 blocks a causal ruling, but it does not erase the co-occurrence. Confounding is exactly the case that 'association-only' exists for. The flagged argument mixes up 'cannot attribute specifically' (not causal) with 'no association shown' (unknown).

H3 is a conjunction: 2026 valves are defective AND Pellacott performed the leak tests its certificates record AND the method misses the defect. C10 is an independent observation that directly falsifies the second part. LT-04 has been out of service since 9 Jan 2026 and its last cycle was 18 Dec 2025. No other rig on site has a VA-220 program. All 31 checked 2026 tables match recycled November 2025 sequences, and no backup rig or its logs were produced. C5's failure to replicate the method matters only when C10 is absent. With C10 on the optimal read path, the evidence counts against H3, not merely fails to discriminate. The flag's own justification supports the key.
